text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Currency exchange, especially the strong dollar, demands additional cut of 950 million markka in the budget, Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto says.
- Finance Minister Niinisto is reported to be laying ground for a stringent election budget for 1999 already now. Stringent expenses cut are meant to stop the state running a deficit.

- The main opposition party, the Centre Party, is preparing to reject Finland's entry to European economic and monetary union's (EMU), if important trade partners Britain and Sweden decide to stay outside.
KAUPPALEHTI
- Finnish National Fund for Research and Development (SITRA) and financing institution CapMan have formed largest Finnish capital financing fund directed to company investments.
- State debt increased by 25.5 million markka from year- end 1996.
- Deposits on low-rate bank accounts have increased by 10 billion markka in January-June 1997, Bank of Finland says.
- Profitability in electricity sector has risen to the level of boom years, sector says couple of good years are still ahead.
AAMULEHTI
- Finnish paper workers' union is after all ready to consider participating in negotiations on a broad pay deal, union's chariman Jarmo Lahteenmaki says.
- No more posts for police will be created, despite demands of Interior Minister Jan-Erik Enestam.
- Foreign, justice and interior ministries spending for 1998 were agreed at government budget talks late Tuesday.
- Planned loans with share options for Merita bank's management, cancelled because of wide public protest, would have earned them already 70 million markka.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Behind government's planned budget are only attempts to cut taxes, not to slow down state running on deficit, main opposition party Centre party says.
- Of Finnish entrepreneurs 40 percent are women, whereas in other European countries they amount to 25-35 percent, local representative of entrepeneurs says.
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen has named a group to study effects of demographics on job markets and prepare Finnish job markets for the future.
-- Nora Hallberg, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 292
